meaning: Placed at the start of a sentence to state the speaker's feeling (surprise, regret, joy, etc.) about the fact that follows. Like “To my surprise, ...” or “Sadly, ...”.
connection: Emotion i-adjective / na-adjective + な / verb ta-form + ことに(は)

senses.label: Feeling (adjective)
senses.meaning: You state your feeling first, then the fact that caused it. Like “Sadly, ...” or “Luckily, ...”. It usually follows emotion adjectives such as 「残念な」, 「嬉しい」, 「不思議な」, and 「ありがたい」. Adding 「は」 makes it more formal and emphatic.
senses.connection: i-adjective dictionary form / na-adjective + な + ことに(は): 残念なことに, 嬉しいことに, 幸いなことに, ありがたいことに
examples: Sadly, the fireworks festival was canceled because of rain.
To my delight, my daughter got into her first-choice university.
Fortunately, no one was injured.

senses.label: Feeling (verb)
senses.meaning: Follows the ta-form of emotion verbs such as 「驚いた」, 「困った」, and 「あきれた」. Like “Surprisingly, ...” or “The trouble is, ...”. What follows is usually an unexpected fact.
senses.connection: Emotion verb ta-form + ことに(は): 驚いたことに, 困ったことに, あきれたことに
examples: Surprisingly, I heard he finished that book in one night.
The trouble was, my passport had expired.
Unbelievably, he didn't even apologize.

notes: It only follows words of emotion or evaluation. You can't use ordinary action verbs like 「食べた」 or 「行く」.
The second half must be an objective fact, not a wish, command, or guess. ✕「残念なことに、行きましょう」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ないことには」 (“unless ...”), which is a condition.
Fairly formal. In conversation, 「驚いたのは〜だ」 is more common.

daily.title: Sharing good news with a friend
daily.description: Telling a friend about a nice surprise, you say how you feel first.
daily.example: Guess what — I'm getting a raise starting next month!

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Accident reports often use 「幸いなことに」 to say no one was hurt.
daily.example: Fortunately, all the passengers were safe.

daily.title: Writing a diary
daily.description: Recording something surprising in a diary or blog.
daily.example: To my surprise, I ran into a friend from ten years ago at the station.

work.title: Giving a client bad news
work.description: To soften an unfavorable result, express regret first.
work.example: Unfortunately, we were unable to meet your request this time.

work.title: Writing a survey report
work.description: Pointing out an unexpected finding in a report.
work.example: Surprisingly, the younger the generation, the more highly they rated print newspapers.

etymology: 「こと」 is a formal noun meaning “this matter”, and 「に」 means “as for”. It's thought to have originally meant “as for this (surprising, sad, etc.) matter”, then became fixed as a sentence opener for stating feelings. 「は」 adds emphasis.

similar.title: 〜ないことには
similar.explanation: 「〜ないことには」 follows the negative form of a verb and means “unless ..., (you can't) ...”, a condition. 〜ことに(は) expresses the speaker's feeling, and what follows is a fact.

similar.title: 〜ことか
similar.explanation: 「〜ことか」 comes at the end of a sentence and strongly exclaims how intense something is (「どんなに嬉しかったことか」). 〜ことに(は) comes at the start and gives the feeling before the fact.

similar.title: 〜のは〜だ (emphasis)
similar.explanation: 「驚いたのは、〜ことだ」 expresses something similar and is more common in speech. 〜ことに(は) is shorter and more formal.

meaning: Gives one reason at hand, like “since ..., (let's) ...”. It's usually followed by a suggestion, decision, or request.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form / na-adjective + な・である / noun + の・である + ことだし

senses.label: Suggestion
senses.meaning: Gives a reason at hand and naturally leads into a suggestion. Like “Since ..., let's ...”. The second half is often 「〜よう」, 「〜ましょう」, or 「〜たらどう」. The tone is light and hints there are other reasons too.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / i-adjective + ことだし, 〜よう／〜ましょう (often with 「も」: 雨もやんだことだし)
examples: The rain has stopped, so shall we head out soon?
Now that everyone's here, let's start the meeting.
It's nice out, so let's walk to the park.

senses.label: Explaining a decision
senses.meaning: Gives the reason for a decision you've made. Like “Since ..., I've decided to ...”. The second half is often 「〜ことにした」, 「〜つもりだ」, a goodbye, or a request.
senses.connection: Plain form + ことだし／ことですし + decision, leave-taking, or request
examples: My kids have grown up, so I decided to go back to work.
It's getting late, so I'll be going now.
I just got paid, so I'm planning to buy a new computer.

notes: The second half is usually the speaker's will, a suggestion, or a request. It isn't used just to describe objective past facts.
It often pairs with 「も」 (「雨もやんだことだし」), hinting that there are other reasons too.
「ことですし」 is the polite form. It's softer than 「から」 or 「し」, and is mostly spoken.
「〜ことだから」 usually follows a person and means “knowing what he's like”. That's a different pattern.

daily.title: Deciding where to go with friends
daily.description: After a meal, suggesting a change of scene.
daily.example: We're full now — want to take a little walk?

daily.title: Weekend at home
daily.description: On a nice day, suggesting a chore to your family.
daily.example: It's nice out, so let's air out the futons.

work.title: Opening a meeting
work.description: The chair confirms everyone is here and starts.
work.example: Since everyone is here, let's get started.

work.title: Before going home
work.description: At a good stopping point, suggesting to coworkers that you wrap up.
work.example: We've reached a good stopping point, so let's call it a day.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「こと」, the copula 「だ」, and the conjunction 「し」, which lists reasons. 「こと」 sums up the situation as “this matter”, and 「し」 hints that there's more than one reason, so it sounds softer than 「から」.

similar.title: 〜し
similar.explanation: 「〜し」 also lists reasons and can stack several (「安いし、おいしいし」). 〜ことだし usually gives just one situation at hand, followed by a suggestion or decision.

similar.title: 〜ことだから
similar.explanation: 「〜ことだから」 usually follows a person (「彼のことだから」) and makes a guess based on their character. 〜ことだし follows a situation and leads to a suggestion.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: 「〜から」 states a reason objectively, and anything can follow. 〜ことだし is lighter and softer, and is usually followed by an intention or invitation.

title: 〜次第 (as soon as)
meaning: As soon as the first thing happens, the second is done right away. Like “as soon as ...”. Mostly used in formal business settings.
connection: Verb masu-stem / suru-verb stem + 次第

senses.label: As soon as
senses.meaning: As soon as the first thing happens, you do the second right away. Like “as soon as ..., I'll ...”. The second half is a deliberate action, such as contacting, leaving, or starting. The tone is formal, common in business and announcements.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 次第: 分かり次第, 決まり次第, でき次第, 着き次第
examples: We will contact you as soon as we know the details.
We'll leave as soon as we're ready.
Please check in at the reception as soon as you arrive at the venue.

senses.label: Noun + 次第
senses.meaning: Follows the noun part of suru-verbs such as 「到着」, 「完成」, 「入荷」, and 「終了」, with the same meaning. Common in notices and announcements.
senses.connection: suru-verb stem + 次第: 到着次第, 入荷次第, 完成次第, 終了次第
examples: Items will be shipped in order as soon as they come in stock.
I'll send you the report as soon as the meeting is over.
Please call me as soon as you arrive.

notes: The second half must be a deliberate action (contacting, leaving, etc.), not something that just happens.
Not used for past events: ✕「駅に着き次第、電話した」. Say 「着くとすぐ電話した」 instead.
It looks like 「次第で」 (“depending on”) and 「次第です」 (“that's how it came about”). Check whether it follows a masu-stem, a noun, or a plain form.
「次第に」 is an adverb meaning “gradually” and has nothing to do with this pattern.

daily.title: Waiting for results
daily.description: Promising a friend you'll get in touch once you know.
daily.example: I'll let you know as soon as I hear the results.

daily.title: A notice when shopping online
daily.description: A store explains out-of-stock items ship once they arrive.
daily.example: Your order will be shipped as soon as it comes in stock.

work.title: Replying to a client email
work.description: You can't answer yet, so you promise to reply once you've checked.
work.example: I will get back to you as soon as I have confirmed this.

work.title: Reporting from a business trip
work.description: Telling your boss you'll report as soon as you arrive.
work.example: I will report to you as soon as I arrive.

etymology: 「次第」 originally meant “order, sequence”. From “in order” it came to mean “(once the first thing is done) then next ...”, showing that the second action follows right away.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: 「〜たとたん」 means something unexpected happened the moment something else did. The second half is a past fact. With 〜次第, the second half is something the speaker will do, never the past.

similar.title: 〜や否や
similar.explanation: 「〜や否や」 is very literary and describes actions in the past that followed immediately. 〜次第 is for future plans and announcements.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「〜てから」 only shows order (“after ...”), with no sense of “right away”.

title: 〜次第だ・〜次第で (depending on)
meaning: Shows that how things turn out depends entirely on the first part. Like “it depends on ...” or “it's up to ...”.

senses.label: Depends on
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, it means the outcome is decided by what comes before. Like “it all depends on ...” or “it's up to ...”. Common phrases: 「あなた次第だ」, 「やり方次第だ」.
senses.connection: Noun + 次第だ／次第です
examples: Whether you pass depends on your own effort.
Whether you go or not is up to you.
Life is what you make of it.

senses.label: Depending on
senses.meaning: In the middle of a sentence, it means “depending on ..., (the result will be) ...”. The second half is often 「変わる」, 「決める」, or 「〜にも〜にもなる」. 「次第では」 hints “depending on how it goes, ... could even happen”.
senses.connection: Noun + 次第で(は)／次第によって(は): 天気次第で, 結果次第では, 使い方次第で
examples: Let's decide tomorrow's plans depending on the weather.
Depending on how you use them, tools can be handy or dangerous.
Depending on the results, we may revise the plan.

notes: It follows a noun. After a verb masu-stem it means “as soon as” (「決まり次第」), so be careful.
「次第では」 and 「次第によっては」 stress that, depending on the situation, a certain result could happen.
It can also modify a noun: 「運次第の勝負」 (a game that depends on luck).
「〜した次第です」 explains circumstances; it doesn't mean “depends on”.

daily.title: Letting a friend decide
daily.description: When a friend asks where to go, you leave it to them.
daily.example: It's up to you where we go.

daily.title: Planning the weekend
daily.description: Talking with family and deciding based on the weather.
daily.example: Let's decide whether to go to the beach depending on the weather.

daily.title: Encouraging a study buddy
daily.description: Telling a friend that progress comes from daily effort.
daily.example: Whether you get good at it depends on your daily practice.

work.title: Business negotiations
work.description: Telling the other side the price is negotiable depending on quantity.
work.example: We are open to discussing the price depending on the quantity you order.

work.title: Project meeting
work.description: Explaining the schedule may change based on results.
work.example: Depending on the survey results, the schedule may change.

etymology: 「次第」 originally meant “order, sequence”. From “unfolding in order” it came to mean “depending on how ... goes”, showing that the result changes with the first part.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「〜によって」 objectively says “varies by ...” (「国によって習慣が違う」). 〜次第で stresses “entirely decided by ...”, often implying that success or failure rests on it.

similar.title: 〜にかかっている
similar.explanation: 「〜にかかっている」 also means “depends on”, but it's stronger and more formal. 〜次第だ is more conversational and more common.

similar.title: 〜に応じて
similar.explanation: 「〜に応じて」 means “adjusting according to ...”, mostly for amounts and degrees. 〜次第で focuses on “the result is decided by ...”.

similar.title: 〜次第 (as soon as)
similar.explanation: Same form, but it follows a verb masu-stem and means “as soon as” (「分かり次第」).

title: 〜次第だ (circumstances)
meaning: Used to formally explain how something came about or why you're doing something. Like “that is why ...” or “I am writing to ...”.
connection: Verb plain form (usually ta-form) / 〜という・〜ような + 次第だ／次第です

senses.label: Explaining circumstances
senses.meaning: Formally explains to someone what happened or why you're doing something. Like “that is why ...” or “I am writing to ...”. Mostly used in letters and business. Common forms: 「〜た次第です」, 「〜ている次第です」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / te-iru form + 次第です (でございます)
examples: I am contacting you because we would like you to confirm this as soon as possible.
I have come to apologize about the other day.
We are sincerely grateful for everyone's cooperation.

senses.label: Thus / so
senses.meaning: 「という次第で」 and 「ような次第で」 pick up the situation just described and lead to a conclusion. Like “For these reasons, ...” or “So, ...”.
senses.connection: 〜という／〜ような + 次第で (です)
examples: For these reasons, this trip has been canceled.
As explained above, we would appreciate your understanding.
That's the situation, so please wait a little longer.

notes: Formal and written in tone. Used in business emails, speeches, and letters of apology; not between friends.
It often pairs with 「〜たく」 (“wishing to ...”): 「お願いしたく、ご連絡した次第です」.
It follows a verb plain form and only explains circumstances. It doesn't mean “depends on”, so don't confuse it with 「あなた次第です」.
「事の次第」 means “how things happened”, as in 「事の次第を説明する」.

daily.title: Reading a formal letter
daily.description: In a letter to a teacher or elder, explaining why you're writing.
daily.example: I am writing to express my thanks to you, sensei.

daily.title: Reading an apology notice
daily.description: A store posts an apology on its website.
daily.example: We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience we have caused.

work.title: Opening a business email
work.description: Explaining your purpose when contacting a client for the first time.
work.example: I am writing to introduce our new service.

work.title: Explaining a delay to a client
work.description: Explaining why a delivery is late.
work.example: For the reasons above, delivery will be delayed by one week.

etymology: 「次第」 originally meant “order”, then “how things unfold, the course of events” (「事の次第」). 「〜次第です」 means “that's how it came about”, and gradually became a formal way to explain.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: 「〜わけだ」 draws a logical conclusion (“no wonder”, “in other words”). 〜次第だ formally explains how your own actions came about and is more polite.

similar.title: 〜次第だ・〜次第で (depending on)
similar.explanation: That one follows a noun and means “depends on”. This pattern follows a verb plain form or 「という」 and gives the circumstances.

similar.title: 〜始末だ
similar.explanation: 「〜始末だ」 means that after a lot of trouble, things ended badly, with criticism. 〜次第だ is neutral and only explains what happened.

meaning: After a long time of thinking, effort, or difficulty, some result is finally reached. Like “after (much) ..., finally ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form / noun + の + 末(に)

senses.label: After ..., finally
senses.meaning: After a lot of thinking, effort, or ups and downs, a result is reached. Like “after much ..., finally ...”. It usually follows words that involve a process, such as 「悩む」, 「考える」, 「迷う」, 「苦労」, and 「議論」. Fairly formal.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 末(に) / noun + の末(に): 悩んだ末に, 考えた末, 苦労の末, 話し合いの末
examples: After agonizing over it, I decided to quit my job.
After lengthy discussions, they finally reached an agreement.
After failing many times, they succeeded in developing a new drug.

senses.label: 〜末の + noun
senses.meaning: 「〜末の + noun」 modifies a noun: “a ... reached after ...”. Examples: 「考えた末の結論」, 「苦労の末の成功」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / noun + の + 末の + noun
examples: This is a decision I made after months of thought.
It was a discovery that came after ten years of research.

notes: The second half is the final result, usually in the past tense, describing what already happened.
The result can be good or bad, but the focus is on the hard process. For bad results, 「〜あげく」 is more common.
It can also be written in kana: 「すえ」. 「月末」 and 「年の末」 mean “the end (of a period)” and are not this pattern.
Fairly formal. In conversation, people often say 「さんざん考えて、結局〜」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a hero choosing after long hesitation.
daily.example: After wavering for a long time, he chose the road back to his hometown.

daily.title: Explaining a choice to a friend
daily.description: Saying you compared a lot before deciding what to buy.
daily.example: After comparing all sorts of options, I went with this computer.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting the outcome of negotiations or deliberations.
work.example: After three days of talks, the two countries issued a joint statement.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: Explaining a decision made after careful review.
work.example: After careful consideration, we have decided to postpone this project.

etymology: 「末」 originally meant “the tip of a tree, the end”, and came to mean “the last part, the end of something”. 「〜た末に」 means “at the end of ...”, showing the outcome after a process.

similar.title: 〜あげく
similar.explanation: 「〜あげく」 also means “after ..., in the end”, but the result is usually bad or troubling, with dissatisfaction. 〜末 can be good or bad and is more neutral and formal.

similar.title: 〜結果
similar.explanation: 「〜結果」 simply shows cause and effect: “as a result of ...”. 〜末 stresses a long, hard process.

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: 「〜たあとで」 only shows time order (“after ...”), with no sense of effort or difficulty.

meaning: Driven by a feeling or situation, you can't stop yourself from doing something. Like “can't help ...ing” or “can't help but ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form + ではいられない (する→しないではいられない)

senses.label: Can't help ...ing
senses.meaning: You can't control yourself and do something without meaning to. Like “can't help ...ing” or “can't help but ...”. Mostly about the speaker's own feelings and impulses.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ではいられない: 笑わないでは, 泣かないでは, 思い出さないでは
examples: Anyone who sees that movie can't help but cry.
What he said was so funny that I couldn't help laughing.
Whenever I see that photo, I can't help thinking of my hometown.

senses.label: Can't just stand by
senses.meaning: Out of a sense of duty or justice, you can't just stand by and must do something. Like “can't help but ...” or “feel I have to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ではいられない: 手を貸さないでは, 注意しないでは
examples: When I see someone in trouble, I can't help but lend a hand.
If a child is doing something dangerous, I can't help but warn them.

notes: Same meaning as 「〜ずにはいられない」. 「〜ないでは」 is a bit more conversational; 「〜ずには」 is more formal.
With a third-person subject, add 「ようだ」, 「らしい」, or 「のだ」 at the end: 「彼は文句を言わないではいられないようだ」.
「する」 becomes 「しないではいられない」. With 「ずには」, it's 「せずにはいられない」.
In writing, you may also see 「〜ないではおれない」.

daily.title: Watching a game with friends
daily.description: When the game is exciting, you can't help cheering.
daily.example: With a game this good, I can't help but cheer!

daily.title: Recommending a novel
daily.description: Telling a friend you can't put a book down.
daily.example: With this novel, you can't stop reading.

daily.title: Seeing bad manners
daily.description: When someone cuts in line, you can't help saying something.
daily.example: When I see people cutting in line, I can't help saying something.

work.title: Farewell party speech
work.description: Expressing gratitude at a farewell party.
work.example: When I think of all your support, I can't help but feel grateful.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A commentator expresses concern about a social issue.
work.example: Looking at the current state of young people, I can't help worrying about the future.

etymology: Made of the negative 「ない」, 「で」 (state), the topic particle 「は」, and 「いられない」, the negative potential of 「いる」. Literally “can't stay in a state of not doing ...”, which came to mean “can't help doing”.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning. 「ず」 is a classical negative, so it sounds more formal; 〜ないではいられない is a bit more conversational.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: 「〜てたまらない」 means a feeling or sensation is unbearably strong (「嬉しくてたまらない」). 〜ないではいられない focuses on “can't help doing something”.

similar.title: 〜ずにはおかない／〜ないではおかない
similar.explanation: 「〜ないではおかない」 means “will definitely ...” or “is bound to make ...”, with strong will or inevitability. 〜ないではいられない is an impulse you can't control.

meaning: Gives a cause you can't be sure of. Like “maybe because ...”. Often leads to a bad result.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form / na-adjective + な / noun + の + せいか

senses.label: Guessing a cause (negative)
senses.meaning: Guesses an uncertain cause for the situation that follows. Like “maybe because ...”. The result is usually something bad.
senses.connection: Plain form / na-adjective + な / noun + の + せいか: 疲れたせいか, 年のせいか, 寝不足のせいか
examples: Maybe because I didn't sleep enough, I have a headache today.
Maybe it's my age, but I get tired easily these days.
Maybe because I ate too much yesterday, my stomach feels off.

senses.label: Guessing a cause (neutral)
senses.meaning: When the cause is uncertain, it can also lead to a good or neutral result. Like “probably because ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + の + せいか + neutral or positive result
examples: Maybe it's the medicine, but I feel much better.
Maybe it's because it's spring, but people in town look cheerful.

senses.label: 気のせいか
senses.meaning: 「気のせいか」 is a set phrase meaning “maybe it's just me”. It shows the speaker isn't sure about their own impression.
senses.connection: 気のせいか、〜 (ように見える／気がする)
examples: Maybe it was just me, but she looked a bit down.

notes: With 「せいか」, the cause is only a guess. For a definite cause, use 「〜せいで」 (bad result) or 「〜おかげで」 (good result).
It can be used for good results, but it's more often used for bad ones.
Usually written in kana; the kanji 「所為」 is rare.

daily.title: Feeling unwell
daily.description: Telling your family the possible cause of your sore throat.
daily.example: Maybe because I sat under the air conditioner too long, my throat hurts.

daily.title: Worrying about a friend
daily.description: A friend seems thinner; you ask if they've been busy.
daily.example: Have you lost a bit of weight lately? Maybe because you've been busy?

daily.title: Weather and mood
daily.description: After days of rain, you share how you feel.
daily.example: Maybe because it's been raining for days, I feel kind of down.

work.title: Analyzing sales data
work.description: Guessing why customer numbers dropped in a meeting.
work.example: Maybe because of the unseasonable weather, customer numbers have been sluggish this month.

work.title: News report
work.description: News guesses the cause of a trend.
work.example: Perhaps because of the weak yen, more tourists are coming from overseas.

etymology: 「せい」 is written 「所為」 in kanji and means “the cause, the fault”, usually of something bad. Adding the uncertain 「か」 makes it “maybe it's because of ...”.

similar.title: 〜せいで
similar.explanation: 「〜せいで」 states the cause firmly, often with blame. 〜せいか is just a guess and sounds milder.

similar.title: 〜おかげで
similar.explanation: 「〜おかげで」 gives the cause of a good result, with gratitude. With 〜せいか the cause is uncertain, and the result is usually bad.

similar.title: 〜からか・〜のか
similar.explanation: 「〜からか」 and 「〜のか」 can also give an uncertain cause, in a neutral tone. 〜せいか is more often used for bad results.

meaning: The result matches someone's status, ability, or effort. Like “as you'd expect from ...” or “no wonder ...”. It carries praise.
connection: Noun / verb or adjective plain form (na-adjective + な) + だけあって

senses.label: As expected of
senses.meaning: The status, position, or reputation in the first part matches the result in the second. Like “as you'd expect from ...”. Often paired with 「さすが」, and the second half is positive.
senses.connection: Noun + だけあって: さすがプロだけあって, 一流ホテルだけあって
examples: As you'd expect from a professional chef, every dish is delicious.
As you'd expect from a top hotel, the service is impeccable.
He's a former athlete, so no wonder he still runs fast.

senses.label: Worth the effort
senses.meaning: Because of the effort or cost put in, you get a matching result. Like “no wonder ...” or “sure enough ...”.
senses.connection: Verb plain form / i-adjective / na-adjective + な + だけあって: 練習しただけあって, 高いだけあって, 有名なだけあって
examples: She practiced every day, and it showed — her piano playing was superb.
These shoes are expensive, but that's why they're so comfortable.
It's famous for a reason — there was a long line in front of the shop.

notes: The second half is a positive evaluation. Don't use it when the result is bad.
It often pairs with 「さすが(に)」 for stronger praise.
At the end of a sentence, say 「〜だけのことはある」 or 「〜だけある」, with a similar meaning.
The second half evaluates a fact. It can't be a wish or command.

daily.title: Eating great food while traveling
daily.description: Praising authentic food in the place it comes from.
daily.example: As you'd expect from where it was born, this ramen is really good.

daily.title: Complimenting a friend
daily.description: A friend who lived abroad has great pronunciation.
daily.example: You lived in America, so no wonder your English pronunciation is so good.

daily.title: After shopping
daily.description: You bought something pricey and feel it was worth it.
daily.example: It was expensive, but that's why this bag is so sturdy.

work.title: Praising a coworker
work.description: Praising an experienced coworker for handling problems quickly.
work.example: As you'd expect from a veteran, she deals with problems fast.

work.title: Product review
work.description: A review praises a new product's performance.
work.example: As you'd expect from the latest model, its processing speed is much faster.

etymology: 「だけ」 comes from the noun 「丈（たけ）」, meaning “length, extent”. 「だけあって」 literally means “having a matching extent”, which came to mean “living up to one's status or effort”.

similar.title: 〜だけに
similar.explanation: 「〜だけに」 stresses “precisely because ..., all the more ...”, and the result can be good or bad. 〜だけあって is only for praise: “as you'd expect from ...”.

similar.title: 〜だけのことはある
similar.explanation: Usually at the end of a sentence: you state the result first, then say “it lives up to its name”. 〜だけあって comes mid-sentence, with the reason first.

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: 「〜にしては」 means the result doesn't match the status (“for a ..., it's quite ...”). 〜だけあって means it does match.

meaning: Precisely because of the first situation, the result or feeling is even stronger. Like “precisely because ..., all the more ...”.
connection: Noun / verb or adjective plain form (na-adjective + な) + だけに

senses.label: All the more because
senses.meaning: Because of the status or situation in the first part, the second is even more so. Like “precisely because ..., all the more ...”. The result can be good or bad.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + だけに: 初めての優勝だけに, 真面目なだけに, 観光地だけに
examples: Since it's their first championship, the joy is all the greater.
Precisely because he's so serious, he worries too much about a single failure.
Since it's a tourist spot, everywhere is crowded on weekends.

senses.label: All the more (disappointed) because
senses.meaning: The first part is an expectation or effort, and the second is a result that falls short, with regret or disappointment. Like “because ..., it's all the more ...”. A common phrase: 「期待が大きかっただけに」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / i-adjective past form + だけに: 期待していただけに, 頑張っただけに
examples: Because my hopes were so high, I was all the more disappointed with the result.
Since I worked so hard to prepare, it's all the more disappointing that it was canceled.

notes: The result can be good or bad. 「〜だけあって」 is only for positive evaluations.
It often goes with 「なおさら」, 「ひとしお」, or 「かえって」.
Don't confuse it with 「だけに」 meaning “only to ...”: 「あなただけに話す」 (I'll tell only you).
「〜だけにとどまらない」 means “not limited to ...” and is also not this pattern.

daily.title: Talking about a game with a friend
daily.description: When your team loses after leading.
daily.example: We were winning right up to the end, so losing like that really stings.

daily.title: Going out on a holiday
daily.description: Sighing at the crowds during a long weekend.
daily.example: It's a long weekend, so it's crowded everywhere you go.

daily.title: Getting a present
daily.description: When you get an unexpected gift.
daily.example: Because I wasn't expecting it, I was really happy.

work.title: Project wrap-up meeting
work.description: Expressing regret about a canceled project.
work.example: Since we spent so much time preparing, it's very disappointing that it's been canceled.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting on the impact of a big company's scandal.
work.example: Precisely because it's a major company, the impact of this scandal is huge.

etymology: 「だけ」 comes from 「丈（たけ）」, meaning “extent”, and 「に」 shows cause. Literally “because it has that extent”, which came to mean “precisely because ..., all the more ...”.

similar.title: 〜だけあって
similar.explanation: Only for praise: “as you'd expect from ...”. 〜だけに can be good or bad and stresses “all the more”.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: 「〜からこそ」 stresses the reason (“precisely because”) but doesn't necessarily mean “all the more”. 〜だけに focuses on “and so even more ...”.

similar.title: 〜だけ (limiting)
similar.explanation: In 「彼にだけ話した」, 「だけ」 means “only”, used with the particle 「に」. It's not this pattern.

meaning: The result matches someone's status, reputation, or effort. Like “it lives up to ...” or “it was worth ...”.
connection: Noun / verb or adjective plain form (na-adjective + な) + だけのことはある

senses.label: Lives up to its name
senses.meaning: You describe the result first, then judge that it matches the status or reputation. Like “just what you'd expect from ...” or “it lives up to its name”. Often paired with 「さすが」.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + だけのことはある: さすが有名店だけのことはある, 長年住んでいるだけのことはある
examples: This ramen is really good. Just what you'd expect from a famous shop.
His Japanese is perfect. That's what ten years in Japan will do.

senses.label: Worth the effort
senses.meaning: Because of the effort or cost put in, the result is fitting. Like “it was worth ...” or “it paid off”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / i-adjective + だけのことはある (あった): 山を登っただけのことはあった, 高いだけのことはある
examples: The view is amazing. It was worth climbing the mountain for three hours.
This coat is warm. It's worth the high price.
My daily practice paid off — I was able to give it my all in the match.

notes: Usually at the end of a sentence: state the result, then evaluate it with this pattern.
Only used for positive evaluations.
「〜だけのことはあって」 can go mid-sentence, like 「〜だけあって」.
In 「やるだけのことはやった」 (I did everything I could), 「だけのこと」 shows a limit. It's not this pattern.

daily.title: Great food after a long wait
daily.description: You waited in line a long time and it was worth it.
daily.example: It was worth waiting in line for an hour. It's amazing!

daily.title: At a concert
daily.description: Impressed after seeing a famous singer live.
daily.example: Her live voice was breathtaking. Just what you'd expect from a world-class singer.

work.title: Evaluating a partner company
work.description: Acknowledging the work of a professional firm.
work.example: The finish is meticulous. Just what you'd expect from the industry leader.

work.title: After new-hire training
work.description: Praising a new hire who improved a lot after training.
work.example: His phone manner has improved dramatically. The training really paid off.

etymology: 「だけ」 comes from 「丈（たけ）」, meaning “extent”, and 「こと」 means “such a thing, value”. Literally “has a value to match”, which came to mean “lives up to its name” or “wasn't in vain”.

similar.title: 〜だけあって
similar.explanation: Goes mid-sentence, with the reason first and the result after. 〜だけのことはある usually ends the sentence, with the result first and the judgment after.

similar.title: 〜だけに
similar.explanation: 「〜だけに」 means “precisely because ..., all the more ...”, and the result can be good or bad. 〜だけのことはある is only for praise.

similar.title: 〜甲斐がある
similar.explanation: 「〜甲斐がある」 means an action was rewarded (「頑張った甲斐があった」), focusing on the payoff of effort. 〜だけのことはある can also be about status or reputation.

meaning: Even if you do the first thing, you won't get the result you want. Like “even if ..., it's no use”. It can also mean “when ... is done, (next) ...”.

senses.label: Even if ..., no use
senses.meaning: Even if you did the first thing, you wouldn't get the result you want. The second half is usually a negative judgment. Like “even if ..., (it won't) ...”. Often with 「いくら」, 「どんなに」, or 「今さら」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ところで + negative judgment (〜ない／無駄だ／どうにもならない)
examples: Even if I apologize now, they probably won't forgive me.
No matter how much I hurry, I won't make it now.
Even if we talk to him about it, I don't think anything will change.

senses.label: Even if ..., only
senses.meaning: With 「せいぜい」, 「〜ぐらいだ」, or 「たいしたことはない」 after it, it means “even if ..., it's only so much”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ところで、せいぜい〜だ／たいして〜ない
examples: Even if I'm late, it'll only be five minutes at most.
Even if I fail, I don't have much to lose.

senses.label: When ... is done
senses.meaning: Marks the point when one action is finished, before moving on to the next. Like “once ...” or “now that ...”. This use isn't contrastive.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ところで + next action
examples: Now that we've reached a good stopping point, let's take a break.
Once everyone had arrived, we made a toast.

notes: In the “even if” use, the second half can't be a fact that already happened or the speaker's intention.
In conversation, 「〜たって」 is often used with a similar meaning: 「謝ったって無駄だ」.
「聞いたところでは」 (“from what I've heard”) and 「ところで」 at the start of a sentence (“by the way”) are not this pattern.
The “when” use is common for hosts of meetings and parties: 「時間になったところで」.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: When a friend is full of regret, you tell them to let it go.
daily.example: Regretting it now won't change anything.

daily.title: Talking with family
daily.description: When you feel there's no point in saying something.
daily.example: Even if I tell him, he won't listen.

daily.title: Comparing prices
daily.description: Feeling the price difference at another shop is small.
daily.example: Even if you buy it next door, it'll only be about 100 yen different.

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: The chair moves to the next item after enough discussion.
work.example: Now that everyone has shared their views, let's move on to the next item.

work.title: Giving your boss an opinion
work.description: Pointing out that adding staff won't solve the problem.
work.example: Even if we add more people, I don't think we'll make the deadline.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally meant “place”, then a point in time or a situation. 「で」 marks the circumstances. Literally “at the point of having done ...”. From “even having come that far” it took on the contrastive meaning “even if ...”.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: 「〜ても」 is the general “even if”, and anything can follow. With 〜たところで, the second half is usually a negative judgment like “no use” or “only so much”, and it sounds stronger.

similar.title: 〜たって
similar.explanation: In conversation it means about the same as 〜たところで, but is more casual. 〜たところで works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜たところ (result)
similar.explanation: 「〜たところ」 means “when I did ..., I found ...”, a fact that already happened. 〜たところで is hypothetical: “even if I did ...”.

similar.title: 〜としたところで／〜にしたところで
similar.explanation: 「〜としたところで」 follows a noun or a sentence and means “even supposing ...”. It's more formal. 〜たところで follows a verb ta-form.

meaning: Strongly denies that something could happen. Like “there's no way ...” or “... can't possibly ...”. Very casual speech.

senses.label: No way
senses.meaning: The speaker subjectively and strongly judges that something is impossible. Like “there's no way ...”. Often follows potential verbs or verbs like 「できる」, 「わかる」, and 「勝てる」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + っこない: できっこない, 読めっこない, 勝てっこない, 間に合いっこない
examples: There's no way I can solve a problem this hard.
A hundred pages in one day? No way I can read that.
Even if I run now, there's no way I'll make it.

senses.label: Others won't understand
senses.meaning: Common phrases: 「〜にはわかりっこない」 and 「誰も信じっこない」. They mean “they'll never understand / believe”, with frustration or resignation.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + っこない (often with 「わかる」 or 「信じる」)
examples: You could never understand how I feel.
Even if I tell the truth, no one will believe me.

notes: Very casual and emotional. In formal settings, use 「〜わけがない」 or 「〜はずがない」.
It's the speaker's subjective judgment, often used with 「なんて」 or 「こんな」.
It mainly follows potential verbs and ability verbs like 「わかる」 and 「できる」.
In rough speech, you may also hear 「〜っこねえ」.

daily.title: A friend's unrealistic plan
daily.description: When a friend says they'll lose 5 kg in a week.
daily.example: Lose five kilos in one week? There's no way you can do that.

daily.title: A child arguing with a parent
daily.description: A child feels their parent doesn't understand.
daily.example: Mom, you could never understand my problems.

daily.title: Losing heart before a game
daily.description: Feeling hopeless against a strong team.
daily.example: There's no way we can beat a team that strong.

work.title: Grumbling to a coworker
work.description: Complaining about an unreasonable deadline to a close coworker.
work.example: All this by tomorrow? There's no way we'll finish.

work.title: Reading a business column
work.description: A column quotes the doubters an entrepreneur once faced.
work.example: People told me, “A product like that will never sell,” but it turned out to be a huge hit.

etymology: 「っこ」 is thought to share its origin with the 「っこ」 in 「かけっこ」 (a race) and 「にらめっこ」 (a staring contest), meaning “doing that”. Adding 「ない」 gives “that's never going to happen”. It developed in casual speech.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: 「〜わけがない」 judges something impossible based on logic and can be used in more formal settings. 〜っこない is more casual and emotional.

similar.title: 〜はずがない
similar.explanation: 「〜はずがない」 infers impossibility from facts or evidence. 〜っこない is usually a strong, subjective denial.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ものか」 shows the speaker's strong will not to do something (「二度と行くものか」). 〜っこない means “it can't happen”.

meaning: Shows that a change is underway, step by step. Like “is gradually ...ing”. Written language.

senses.label: Change in progress
senses.meaning: Something is gradually changing in one direction, and the change isn't finished yet. Like “is steadily ...ing”. Usually follows change verbs such as 「増える」, 「減る」, 「変わる」, and 「回復する」.
senses.connection: Change verb masu-stem + つつある: 増えつつある, 変わりつつある, 回復しつつある
examples: The number of foreign tourists visiting Japan is increasing.
The global environment is getting worse year by year.
The economy is gradually recovering.

senses.label: Nearing completion
senses.meaning: With result verbs such as 「沈む」, 「消える」, and 「完成する」, it shows something is in the process of reaching that result. Like “is ...ing” or “is about to ...”.
senses.connection: Instantaneous verb masu-stem + つつある: 沈みつつある, 消えつつある, 完成しつつある
examples: The sun is setting into the sea.
The old streetscapes are disappearing little by little.
The new station building is nearing completion.

notes: Written language, common in news, papers, and reports. In everyday speech, 「〜てきている」 or 「〜ている」 is more common.
It generally isn't used with ordinary ongoing actions: ✕「ご飯を食べつつある」.
Forms like 「〜つつあった」 and 「〜つつあり、」 are also common.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reports on a social trend.
daily.example: The population in rural areas is declining.

daily.title: Posting about the season
daily.description: Describing autumn slowly arriving.
daily.example: The trees in town are gradually changing color.

daily.title: Reassuring family and friends
daily.description: Saying a family member's health is improving.
daily.example: My father's health is recovering, so please don't worry.

work.title: Market analysis report
work.description: A report describes market trends.
work.example: The number of electronic payment users is expanding rapidly.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Explaining the research background at the start of a paper.
work.example: In recent years, attitudes toward work have been changing dramatically.

etymology: 「つつ」 is a classical conjunctive particle showing repeated or simultaneous action, and 「ある」 shows existence or continuation. Together they mean “being in the middle of ...”. One theory says it spread in writing when translating the progressive tense of Western languages in the modern era.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 「〜ている」 can show an action in progress or a resulting state, and is common in speech. 〜つつある only shows a change that's underway and not yet complete, and is written language.

similar.title: 〜つつ
similar.explanation: 「〜つつ」 means “while ...ing” or the contrastive “although ...”. 〜つつある shows a change in progress, which is different.

similar.title: 〜一方だ
similar.explanation: 「〜一方だ」 means something keeps moving in one direction, usually a bad trend. 〜つつある just objectively describes a change in progress.

similar.title: 〜てくる
similar.explanation: 「〜てきている」 shows a change gradually becoming visible up to now, and is common in speech. 〜つつある is more formal.

meaning: A feeling or sensation wells up naturally and is very strong, beyond control. Like “terribly ...” or “can't help feeling ...”.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective + くて / na-adjective + で + ならない

senses.label: Strong feelings
senses.meaning: Shows a feeling that's hard to hold back. Like “terribly ...” or “so ... I can't stand it”. Often follows emotion words such as 「心配」, 「残念」, 「悔しい」, and 「寂しい」.
senses.connection: i-adjective + くて / na-adjective + で + ならない: 心配でならない, 残念でならない, 悔しくてならない
examples: My son is coming home late, and I'm terribly worried.
I'm so frustrated that we lost the match.
My beloved teacher has passed away, and I am deeply saddened.

senses.label: Can't help feeling
senses.meaning: Follows spontaneous expressions like 「思える」, 「気がする」, and 「感じられる」. Like “I can't help feeling ...” or “I just can't shake the feeling ...”.
senses.connection: Spontaneous verb te-form + ならない: 思えてならない, 気がしてならない, 気になってならない
examples: I can't help thinking he's lying.
I can't shake the feeling that something bad is going to happen.
I can't stop thinking about what was said that time.

notes: Mainly expresses the speaker's own feelings. For a third person, add 「ようだ」 or 「らしい」.
More formal than 「〜てたまらない」. For physical sensations like 「暑い」 and 「痛い」, 「〜てたまらない」 is more common.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てはならない」 (“must not ...”), which is a prohibition.
「なりません」 is the polite form, common in formal speeches.

daily.title: Worrying about family
daily.description: Your daughter went abroad alone; you confide in a friend.
daily.example: My daughter went overseas on her own, and I'm worried sick about her.

daily.title: Missing home
daily.description: Living far away, you get homesick every autumn.
daily.example: Every autumn, I can't help feeling nostalgic for my hometown.

work.title: Formal speech
work.description: Expressing reluctance to part at a farewell party.
work.example: It is truly regrettable that we must part in this way.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A commentator expresses concern about a policy's impact.
work.example: I can't help but be concerned about the impact this policy will have on regional economies.

etymology: 「ならない」 is the negative of 「なる」 (“to work out, be acceptable”), originally meaning “it won't do, it's unbearable”. 「〜てならない」 literally means “so ... it's unbearable”, and came to mean a feeling too strong to control.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「〜てたまらない」 is more conversational and also works for physical sensations (「暑くてたまらない」). 〜てならない is more formal and is used for feelings that well up and with words like 「思える」.

similar.title: 〜てしょうがない・〜て仕方がない
similar.explanation: The most common in conversation, with a similar meaning. 〜てならない is more formal.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: 「〜てはならない」 is a prohibition: “must not ...”. 〜てならない has no 「は」 and shows a strong feeling. They're completely different.
